passed.title: LazyFrame.rolling windows are right-closed (t - period, t] by default
passed.trap: By default `LazyFrame.rolling` uses `closed='right'`, so each window is `(t - period, t]`. The left edge is excluded, which means `period="2i"` covers 2 index values, not 3. Pass `closed='both'` (or adjust `period`/`offset`) if you need both edges included. The `index_column` must be sorted ascending (within each group when `group_by` is set). The method returns a group-by object, so you must call `.agg(...)` on it.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"t": [1, 2, 3, 4], "v": [1, 1, 1, 1]})

right = lf.rolling("t", period="2i").agg(pl.col("v").sum().alias("s"))
both = lf.rolling("t", period="2i", closed="both").agg(
    pl.col("v").sum().alias("s")
)

print(right.collect().sort("t")["s"].to_list())  # [1, 2, 2, 2]
print(both.collect().sort("t")["s"].to_list())   # [1, 2, 3, 3]

passed.title: LazyFrame.quantile defaults to nearest interpolation, not linear
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.quantile` uses `interpolation='nearest'` by default, so it returns an actual data value rather than an interpolated one. For example, `quantile(0.7)` on `[1, 2, 3, 4]` gives `3.0`, while `interpolation='linear'` gives `3.1`. Code ported from tools that interpolate linearly by default, such as pandas, silently returns a different number. Pass `interpolation='linear'` explicitly when you expect linear quantiles.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

nearest = lf.quantile(0.7).collect().item()
linear = lf.quantile(0.7, interpolation="linear").collect().item()

print(nearest)  # 3.0 (default: nearest)
print(round(linear, 6))  # 3.1 (pandas-style linear)

passed.title: LazyFrame.remove keeps rows where the predicate is null
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.remove` drops only rows where the predicate is exactly True. Rows where it evaluates to `null`, for example a comparison against a null value, are **retained**. This means `remove(cond)` is not the same as `LazyFrame.filter(~cond)`: the filter drops the null row and the remove keeps it. If null rows should also be discarded, add the null case explicitly, e.g. `cond | pl.col(c).is_null()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "bar": [7, None, 1]})
cond = pl.col("bar") >= 5

# null comparison -> null -> row is kept by remove (ids 2 and 3)
print(lf.remove(cond).collect().get_column("id").to_list())

# filter on the negation drops the null row (only id 3)
print(lf.filter(~cond).collect().get_column("id").to_list())

# handle nulls explicitly to remove them too (only id 3)
print(lf.remove(cond | pl.col("bar").is_null()).collect().get_column("id").to_list())

passed.title: Declare the output schema and disable pushdown when a map_batches UDF changes columns or aggregates
passed.trap: With `schema=None`, `LazyFrame.map_batches` assumes the function returns the same schema as its input. A UDF that adds columns therefore fails the default `validate_output_schema=True` check. `predicate_pushdown` defaults to True, so a later filter may be pushed past the UDF. The docstring warns that this changes the results of any aggregation done inside the UDF. Pass the real `schema=` and set `predicate_pushdown=False` when the function aggregates.

passed.title: merge_sorted does not sort: both inputs must already be ascending by the key
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.merge_sorted` is a merge step, not a sort-and-concat. The caller must make sure both frames are sorted **ascending** by `key`; otherwise the docstring says the output will not make sense. The schemas of both frames must be equal, and row order among equal keys is not guaranteed. Call `.sort(key)` on both sides first, or use `pl.concat` followed by a sort.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [3, 1], "v": ["a3", "a1"]})
b = pl.LazyFrame({"k": [2], "v": ["b2"]})

try:
    bad = a.merge_sorted(b, key="k").collect()  # inputs not sorted
    print(bad.get_column("k").to_list(), bad.get_column("k").is_sorted())
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

good = a.sort("k").merge_sorted(b.sort("k"), key="k").collect()
print(good.get_column("k").to_list(), good.get_column("k").is_sorted())

passed.title: LazyFrame.pivot requires on_columns up front
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.pivot` has a required parameter `on_columns` that lists the values of `on` to turn into output columns. Eager-style calls that pass only `on`, `index` and `values` raise `TypeError`. With `aggregate_function=None`, a duplicate `index`/`on` combination raises an error. Because `maintain_order=False` is the default, the output row order is not guaranteed, so sort explicitly.

passed.title: LazyFrame.melt is deprecated: use unpivot with index and on
passed.trap: `LazyFrame.melt` is the pandas-style name and has been deprecated since 1.0.0; it emits a `DeprecationWarning`. Use `LazyFrame.unpivot` instead. The parameters are renamed: `id_vars` becomes `index` and `value_vars` becomes `on`. Passing the old keyword names to `LazyFrame.unpivot` will not work.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import warnings

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"id": [1, 2], "x": [10, 20], "y": [30, 40]})

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("error")
    try:
        lf.melt(id_vars="id", value_vars=["x", "y"])
    except DeprecationWarning:
        print("DeprecationWarning")

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    old = lf.melt(id_vars="id", value_vars=["x", "y"])

new = lf.unpivot(on=["x", "y"], index="id")
print(new.collect().to_dicts())
print(old.collect().equals(new.collect()))

passed.title: LazyFrame.serialize returns binary bytes by default, not JSON
passed.trap: The docstring summary mentions JSON, but the default is `format='binary'`, which returns `bytes`. The `'json'` format is deprecated. Read the result back with `LazyFrame.deserialize` wrapped in `io.BytesIO`. Serialized plans are not stable across Polars versions, so do not use them as a long-term storage format.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import io

lf = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]}).sum()

data = lf.serialize()
print(isinstance(data, bytes), isinstance(data, str))  # True False

restored = pl.LazyFrame.deserialize(io.BytesIO(data))
print(restored.collect().to_dicts())
